#446. Cheaper cars are selling considerably faster than at the beginning of the year

Consumers are concerned about rising fuel prices and affordability — and that could be showing up in how fast the least expensive cars are moving off dealer lots.

From the first quarter to the third, the number of days it took a dealer to sell a vehicle priced between $20,000 and $29,999 dropped 20%, according to data from Edmunds. That pace of selling saw the biggest acceleration of any price segment.

Vehicles priced from $30,000 to $39,999 sold about 18% faster, and the number of days it took to sell the next tier — $40,000 to $49,999 — dropped nearly 12%, according to Edmunds.

All of those price segments also took fewer days to turn than their more expensive counterparts. The lower-priced tiers took under 60 days to move off lots, with the least expensive ones selling the fastest. Every segment of vehicles above $50,000, meanwhile, took more than 60 days to sell.

"If you're a dealer and you have inventory and that price point, you're definitely noticing," said Edmunds Director of Insights Ivan Drury.

Cheaper vehicles may be selling faster, but they're still hard to find. The average listing price for a new vehicle in September was $49,726, according to Cox Automotive.

And, the overall sales numbers for some key segments priced under $40,000 have fallen. This has especially been true for compact cars, which are down roughly 4% since the beginning of 2026, and compact SUVs, down nearly 8% in the same period, according to Cox Automotive.

These different data points seem to be moving in opposite directions. On the one hand, cheaper cars are moving faster off dealer lots. On the other, sales of affordable segments are down.

There are a few reasons for this, according to analysts who follow the industry. One is that there might not be enough lower-priced vehicles on dealer lots in the first place.

"I think there are some supply things going on at that end of the market," said Cox Automotive Deputy Chief Economist Mark Strand. "We have to kind of grade the market on a curve until we see what's going on with fourth-quarter data."

The compact SUV segment, in particular, is suffering from the lack of two popular models.

The Toyota RAV4, which is the most popular SUV in the U.S., has been in short supply at many dealerships this year, as the automaker shifts production to its Kentucky factory, Strand said. The company also has shifted the entire lineup to a hybrid powertrain at a time when hybrids have been in exceptionally high demand.

The other missing SUV is the Ford Escape, which that automaker discontinued to make way for its upcoming midsize EV pickup truck.

The other slow-selling, low-priced segment — compact cars — faces structural inventory challenges, said AutoForecast Solutions Vice President of Global Forecasting Sam Fiorani.

"We've seen the disappearance of affordable, compact new vehicles over the last decade," he said.

Detroit automakers swapped out their lineups of compact coupes and sedans in favor of small crossover SUVs, which tend to carry slightly higher sticker prices than comparably sized passenger cars.

Currently, there is not a single compact passenger sedan for sale by an American manufacturer. Most on the market are Japanese or Korean, with a few German models, such as the Volkswagen Jetta and the Golf hatchback.

"You have all these brands that have just abandoned the marketplace," Fiorani said.

The smallest American passenger cars are the Ford Mustang, General Motors' Chevrolet Corvette, and the midsize Tesla Model 3 sedan, according to AutoForecast Solutions. The firm classifies both the Mustang and the Corvette as sports cars, and as such they occupy a different niche than compact sedans like the Honda Civic or Toyota Corolla.

The Mustang has a starting price of $33,490, the Model 3 starts at $34,990 and the Chevrolet Corvette starts at $71,300. Cars like the Civic, Corolla and Jetta, meanwhile, all start below $25,000.

"Compact vehicle buyers are very price-sensitive," Fiorani said. "And so when the price of gas goes up, that eats into their car payment. That means that they can't afford a $500 or $600 a month car payment, and they have to move into the used market."

Indeed, the wholesale used prices of compact cars have risen and are up more than almost any other segment, according to Cox Automotive. Wholesale prices — the prices vehicles sell for at large auctions, like Cox Automotive's Manheim auction — are indicators for prices overall in the fragmented used-car market.

Along with the rise in prices, auto finance stats show that a historically high number of buyers are stretching to afford cars.

Roughly one in four buyers financing their purchases are getting 84-month loans — a record. Nearly 3 in 10 trade-ins toward new-vehicle purchases carried negative equity in the third quarter, meaning the cars being traded in were worth less than the outstanding balances of the loans on them. Shoppers are often rolling these negative balances into new loans, which pushes up the new payment cost.

Automakers have also been more tightly aligning production with demand to avoid discounting vehicles. Incentives on average are about 6.6% of the average transaction price as of October, according to Cox Automotive. Leasing offers a way to get a car with a lower payment, but leasing rates are also down.

Vehicle trade-in data suggests that many buyers who are snapping up those fast-selling cheaper vehicles are either first-time buyers or are purchasing supplemental vehicles, Edmunds' Drury said.

The subcompact SUV segment is one lower-priced group that has seen sales rise in 2026. That is a segment that attracts a lot of first-time buyers. But this is still a relatively small share of the total car market, Fiorani said.

"It's not the mainstream vehicle that Americans want," he said. "It is the vehicle that entry-level buyers need to get to work, to get to school. ... It's people who don't have families yet."

Repeat buyers are less likely to want to step down into a compact car or SUV, Drury said.

"The moment you get into that other vehicle and it's a little bit smaller, it's not as comfortable, it doesn't fit all your stuff, all your kid's equipment for soccer practice, you're done," he said. "You're not giving up 360 cameras, ventilated seats, heated steering wheels, these niceties that you've become accustomed to. Automakers know that too. Dealers know that."

The truly cash-strapped are either snapping up the relatively few low-priced cars on dealer lots, moving to the used market, or holding on to their cars longer.

"The people who are trying to buy the smaller vehicles are really hurt by the way the economy is at the moment," Fiorani said. "So those people are trying to move into used vehicles or trying to maintain their current vehicle as long as they can. Automakers should be prepared for a softening in the marketplace."

#440. Review: The Ocarina of Time remake is gorgeous, but plays it a little too safe

After careful hands-on testing, we feature our favorite gear and gadgets as Mashable Selects products in our dedicated shopping guides.

Nintendo has audaciously remade The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for a modern audience, and I love thinking about the fact that a bunch of people at Nintendo had to get together and try to nail down exactly what made the game such a monumental success.

Upon its release in 1998, Ocarina of Time for Nintendo 64 was far from the first 3D action-adventure game. It didn't invent lock-on targeting, cinematic storytelling, labyrinthine 3D level design, or any of the other features it's often credited for. What made it special at the time, at least in my view, is that it was arguably the first game to do all of those things really well, at the same time, as part of a cohesive, unforgettable experience.

In trying to capture that magic, Nintendo chose a relatively safe approach in developing this remake. Ocarina of Time for Switch 2, which finally launches on Nov. 5, is strikingly similar to the original on an experiential level. If you've played through the N64 version recently, as I did about six months ago, you might find a somewhat disappointing lack of surprises here.

But I think I can live with a remake that disappoints only because it's a little too much like the original. This is supposed to be a nostalgia trip, after all. I do have some quibbles about the new Ocarina of Time that I'll get to shortly, but broadly speaking, this is a visually brilliant reimagining of one of the most important games ever made. What it lacks in surprise, it makes up for by faithfully and respectfully translating Ocarina into something a bit more modern without compromising what made it great.

As has been clear since Nintendo first started showing off this love letter, the remake does not rock the boat. This is Ocarina of Time, almost exactly as you remember it, but with new visuals and some small revisions along the way.

That means the story, the player's general objectives, dungeon layouts, and boss fights are mostly recreated in a near one-to-one capacity. A few boss fights have been mildly remixed, as have some dungeon puzzles, but having played the N64 release earlier this year, there really weren't very many moments in the remake that felt all that novel. Nintendo's philosophy is clearly that Ocarina was not a game that needed reinvention on a design level.

As thrilling as it would be to see a Final Fantasy VII Remake-level re-interpretation, Ocarina's world, dungeon, and puzzle design were huge parts of what made it so awesome in the first place, so I understand wanting to (mostly) retain those elements.

It's a respectable, if a little boring, approach.

When playing Ocarina of Time for Switch 2, I found myself getting excited every time I encountered something Nintendo did change.

Most prominent, of course, is the visual overhaul. As I explained in a preview last month (before being backed up by an interview with the developers), this version of Ocarina was inspired by and evokes high-end puppetry. Character faces are cartoonish and stylized almost exactly as they were in the N64 original, but their hair and clothing feature extreme levels of realistic detail, as do most of the game's environments.

It's a really neat look that especially pops when you play it on a nice TV rather than watching it in a YouTube window. Individual character personalities, even from minor players like Ingo the ranch-hand or the creepy windmill musician guy, shine through just as much as they did in 1998. You can let go of any lingering fears that the remake sanded down the wacky tone of the original.

If anything, some of the NPCs or monsters are even creepier than before. Wait until you see the remade Happy Mask Salesman, for example. I also enjoy this remake as a demonstration of what the Switch 2 hardware is capable of. Water ripples and fog dissipate based on player actions in a believable manner, texture quality is almost scarily high, and sunlight scatters beautifully on the grass in Hyrule Field. The best part is that it all runs at a near-perfect 60 frames per second.

Nintendo also made some thoughtful alterations to the way Ocarina plays. Namely, Link's movement controls are much snappier and more responsive than they were on N64. The much-talked-about new jump button reduces the likelihood of accidentally launching yourself off a ledge in the wrong direction, and a sprint feature eliminates the need to somersault everywhere without being fast enough to trivialize traversal.

Combat feels juicier and more satisfying, too. The spirit of encounters hasn't changed much; you're still locking on and waiting for an opening before getting in a few strikes. But outstanding hit animations do a lot of work to make those hits feel more impactful.

I'm a little more mixed about how items work in this remake. In the N64 original, you could map three usable items onto the N64's C-buttons, a controller feature that the Switch 2 does not share. Accordingly, Nintendo chose to make it more like Breath of the Wild, with the ability to map one item at a time to a universal "use item" button. The compromise here is that you can open up a quick-swap menu and switch between items fluidly, but it does make enemy encounters that require the use of more than one item in quick succession a little awkward.

I also appreciate the addition of Threads of Time, which functions like a quest log in a contemporary game. In the original Ocarina of Time, players had to rely more on Navi the fairy constantly telling them what to do. Now, you can just open a menu and see all main story and side activities laid out cleanly, with hints on what to do next in each thread. Notably, this does not include objective markers on the map or anything like that, so it feels to me like the information that was already there is being presented in a friendlier way, rather than the game holding the player's hand too much.

As a nice bonus, that means Navi doesn't interrupt exploration nearly as often as she did in the original.

Musically, Ocarina's wonderful score has been fully re-recorded with real instruments and a tasteful smattering of some of the same digital samples that defined the original work. Sprinting across Hyrule Field while an even more triumphant version of that legendary music hits hard, even nearly three decades later. And yes, the new version of the Gerudo Valley theme is fantastic.

As you'd expect, not every alteration Nintendo made to Ocarina is for the best.

While they aren't outright bad, necessarily, I fail to see the need for fully voice-acted cutscenes at critical junctures in the story. In practice, it makes certain sequences longer than they would be if I could button through text at my own pace. I never really felt that the voice acting brought me closer to the events on screen. If anything, because the acting is so cartoony, it took me out of the story at times.

Ocarina has never been known as a particularly difficult game to finish (let's not forget it was designed for kids), but Nintendo redistributed some of the gameplay friction in different directions, resulting in an adventure that's, like, 10 percent easier than it used to be. A small handful of puzzles have been slightly simplified, while enemies don't hit that hard. I was never in danger of hitting a game over screen, but your mileage may vary if you don't have an encyclopedic knowledge of the original game like I do.

It's just kind of a strange decision to make Ocarina easier when more recent entries like Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom are, by Nintendo standards, pretty mean games. I should note, though, that this isn't exactly an across-the-board change. For instance, Great Fairies now ask for large sums of money before they'll give Link upgrades, and since wallet enhancements are tied to finding hidden collectibles, it's now really inadvisable to ignore those. I do like that change, FWIW.

While I greatly enjoyed most of my time with the Ocarina of Time remake, and find most of its changes refreshing in one way or another, there is no denying that just a little more novelty would've made it a better experience. Even just a couple of new NPCs or side quests would've gone a long way.

Even with those misgivings, Nintendo's Ocarina of Time remake for Switch 2 is a sharp and beautiful reminder of what a great game it's always been. The word "resplendent" came to mind when exploring Hyrule.

Dungeons like the Forest Temple and Water Temple still shine as brilliant examples of early-ish 3D level design, and are just as fun to get lost in today as they were in 1998. Most boss battles still provide an excellent closing argument for each dungeon, and it is admittedly nice to play a Zelda game that revolves around using hookshots, boomerangs, and other gadgets and gizmos to complete puzzles again.

I would just recommend creating some distance between yourself and the original N64 version (or its 3DS remaster) before jumping in. The less vivid your memories are, the better a time you'll have. #435. Automakers like Rivian and Ford are ‘democratizing 3D printing’ to reduce costs and increase speed

DETROIT — Automakers including Ford Motor and Rivian Automotive are leaning into a new type of manufacturing line: 3D printing.

Manufacturers say it's helping them reduce costs and increase speed. The technology has been around for decades, but it's becoming more commoditized in the automotive industry, with 3D printers used to create everything from vehicle parts and accessories to tools for assembly plants and testing units for research and development labs.

"At this point, we don't have a choice but to scale up and begin using it through all factions of Rivian," Jonathan Dankenbring, Rivian senior manager of prototype manufacturing, told CNBC during a tour of the automaker's expansive 3D-printing operations in suburban Detroit. "We're going to be democratizing 3D printing for the entire company."

Also known as additive manufacturing, 3D printing can create three-dimensional objects from digital designs by dispensing material layer by layer, much like a traditional printer does with ink on paper. Instead of ink, the machines use a wide variety of materials such as plastics, composites, ceramics and even metals.

Printers can range from hundreds of dollars for hobby-like devices to hundreds of thousands of dollars for specialty equipment, depending on how big the product being produced is and the material it needs. They can produce individual pieces or hundreds of smaller parts in a batch using powders and resins.

Rivian said it has spent more than $5 million on 3D-printing machines, with the cost of materials for the operations growing to about $1.7 million annually.

Dankenbring said despite the costs, the machines typically pay for themselves within a year. He said the technology helps lower supplier tooling costs, streamline logistics expenses and cut production times for parts from weeks to days, if not hours.

"It's well in the millions [for savings], but the main thing is speed for Rivian," Dankenbring said.

The all-electric vehicle company's latest expansion of 3D printing includes adding new machines that can build flexible silicone parts as well as installing a bay of machines at its plant in Normal, Illinois, for employees to print parts on demand.

"3D prints should be readily available for every engineer so that they can make a part and get it in their hands as soon as possible," Dankenbring said.

Rivian has also used the technology for electric-motor models for fluid testing, creating screw guides for tooling and stamping press inserts and some production parts, including trim pieces to fill gaps in some early builds.

There's a similar push underway at larger, more-established automakers like Ford and its crosstown rival General Motors, which have used 3D printing for many years, including in their massive assembly plants.

Instead of having a bay of 3D-printing machines like at Rivian, Ford has departments for additive manufacturing at many of its plants to produce and distribute needed parts. That includes a new vending machine for 3D-printed parts for production of F-150 pickup trucks near its Dearborn, Michigan, headquarters.

"By putting the vending machine up, all the team leaders have access," said Gregory Foresi, a Ford mechanical engineer who ran Ford's 3D-printing lab at the plant from 2024 until last month. "We're able to keep that thing stocked rather than have a bunch of parts laying around in the lab. So that's been pretty huge."

Foresi used roughly two dozen machines to print off thousands of tools, some of which have been designed by employees, such as torque bit sockets, hood jackers and hand tools for smoothing adhesive.

Employees can use an app to request that specific auto parts or tools be printed. Ford's 3D-printing teams help develop them or determine what to produce next, as the machining time to build different parts can range from hours to days, if not weeks.

Foresi said creating the tools with 3D printing has allowed the automaker to uniquely design them when needed, get them faster and, in many cases, receive them at a lower cost.

Ford also has used 3D-printed parts to help keep production running. For example, Foresi said a large machining wheel was needed to maintain assembly line production and the company was able to 3D print the part until a permanent replacement from a supplier was available.

"They didn't perform as well, and it's not really a replacement for the ones that we were purchasing, but they kept the plant running," Foresi said.

Ford said it expects to have 3D labs deployed at more than 23 plants by the end of this year. Its current 3D-printing program has more than 200 machines, and there are additional printers outside the official program, the company said.

GM has used 3D-printed parts for some of its low-volume products in addition to research and development and inside plants, including recently expanding its use of industrial Stratasys printers that can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars based on use case, training and certification.

The Detroit automaker uses 135 components that are 3D-printed for its bespoke Cadillac Celestiq as well as other components for its performance Cadillac Blackwing sedans, including a unique medallion on the manual shifter knob.

Fadi Abro, senior global director of automotive and mobility at 3D-printing company Stratasys, said GM has been a great example of how companies can "standardize and then scale" 3D printing.

"The material properties improved so significantly that the use cases improved," he said, noting the company works with virtually every major automaker. "From a product perspective, we have to get the technology to become faster and more accessible, in an economic sense."

Correction: This story has been updated to reflect that Jonathan Dankenbring is Rivian's senior manager of prototype manufacturing. A previous version of this article misidentified him.

If you were planning to wait until the end of the month to pad your console library, Sony just pulled the trigger early. The PlayStation Store launched its official Black Friday 2026 sale on Nov. 4, bringing discounts of up to 75% across thousands of digital games, DLC packs, and expansions for PS5, PS4, and PS VR2.

The entire promotion runs through Nov. 30 at 11:59 p.m. local time, with Sony scheduling a mid-sale lineup refresh on Nov. 16. Just keep an eye on individual store listings before you buy: several early deals, including high-profile editions of Diablo IV: Lord of Hatred, NBA 2K27, and Silent Hill: Townfall, are scheduled to expire early on Nov. 20 before rotating out.

To save you from combing through thousands of digital store pages, here are our top picks worth grabbing before their limited-time launch prices rotate out.

Grabbing the Diablo IV: Lord of Hatred Standard Edition is easily one of the best values in the entire sale. The bundle packages both major storyline chapters — Vessel of Hatred and Lord of Hatred — into a single release, pitting you directly against Mephisto across the ancient Skovos region with two long-awaited playable classes: the holy Paladin and demon-binding Warlock.

Alongside substantial endgame reworks, transmutation crafting, and gear set bonuses, picking it up grants instant access to an extra stash tab, two bonus character slots for fresh seasonal builds, and three exclusive World of Warcraft decor items.

Picking up Astro Bot during the sale is an absolute no-brainer for anyone who owns a PS5. When Astro’s mothership gets ambushed, and its crew gets scattered across the cosmos, you set off across more than 50 inventive planets to rescue stranded bots and patch the ship back together.

It serves as a love letter to console history — pairing you with iconic PlayStation legends — while also serving as the gold standard for DualSense immersion. Set against the rain-soaked backdrop of 1996 Scotland, it marks the series' first full-length entry played entirely in first person as you explore the fog-covered town of St. Amelia.

Survival leans on tense evasion, desperate melee scraps, and the CRTV — a pocket television that replaces the classic radio to decode eerie static signals and reveal hidden story clues. Backed by a reactive Pilotpriest soundtrack and branching endings, it delivers pure analog dread from start to finish.

The NBA 2K27 Deluxe Edition solves the mode's biggest barrier to entry: the slow, brutal grind to make your custom baller competitive. Dropping 100,000 Virtual Currency (VC) into your balance lets you instantly soup up your MyPLAYER's key attributes, whether that's locking down perimeter defense or draining deep threes, without playing dozens of frustrating, underpowered games.

The included MyCAREER care package keeps that momentum rolling with 25 bundles across six skill boosts, 25 triple-pack Gatorade stamina boosts, a two-hour 2XP coin, and wearable Victor Wembanyama and Caitlin Clark jerseys. If you also like piecing together fantasy lineups in MyTEAM, the five Series 1 packs, Full '27 team selection, and Free Agent pack give you a competitive roster right out of the box.

Grabbing Marvel’s Wolverine Digital Deluxe Edition on sale gives PS5 players the definitive way to experience Insomniac’s brutal, globe-trotting mutant epic. Logan’s journey pulls him back into Team X to stop Bolivar Trask’s mutant-hunting Reavers, slicing through incredible set pieces across Canada, Tokyo, and Madripoor alongside iconic rivals like Omega Red.

The combat lets you build up sheer Rage momentum to shred enemies with fluid adamantium claw strikes and swappable Techniques. Going with the Deluxe Edition loads you up right out of the gate: you get five exclusive suits (including Age of Apocalypse and Savage), five custom claw variants, four bonus Technique Points to kickstart your skill tree, and early unlocks for Logan’s classic brown suit and reflective claws. #429. Apples new 18+ app limits mean little for dating apps, a lot for AI companions

Apple wants to make sure dating apps and AI companions with "sexual or romantic content" are only for people over 18, with new restrictions coming Nov. 16.

Though most dating platforms like Tinder, Hinge, Bumble are already strictly for users over 18, Apple's updated policy requires all apps that include dating and relationship features to have a minimum 18+ age rating in App Store Connect, Apple's command centre for developers managing iOS apps. Devs will also have to disclose whether their app enables real-time location sharing.

Mandatory age rating is a rather incremental update for dating apps, which as mentioned, are usually restricted to users over 18 by the developers themselves. However, as TechCrunch rightly points out, one of the more indeterminate impacts of Apple's policy could be that on minors' use of AI companions.

Artificial intelligence companions from the likes of Replika, Nomi, and the now bankrupt Character.AI, have been widely used by teens for years. As Mashable's Rebecca Ruiz reports, they're platforms specifically designed for emotional intimacy; a 2025 survey of U.S. teens ages 13 to 17 found that 52 percent regularly use AI companions, and 33 percent use them for social interaction and relationships, including friendship, role-playing, emotional support, and romantic interactions.

However, experts have long said AI companions aren't safe for teens under 18, with researchers at Common Sense Media (a U.S. nonprofit providing technology analysis and guidance for parents) rigorously testing Character.AI, Nomi, and Replika for a major 2025 report. James P. Steyer, the nonprofit's founder and CEO, said in a statement at the time, "Social AI companions are not safe for kids. They are designed to create emotional attachment and dependency, which is particularly concerning for developing adolescent brains. Our testing showed these systems easily produce harmful responses including sexual misconduct, stereotypes, and dangerous 'advice' that, if followed, could have life-threatening or deadly real-world impact for teens and other vulnerable people."

In the study, researchers found that "safety measures are easily circumvented," including age gates and terms of service restrictions on teen use. Common Sense Media has since published more research criticising AI companion platforms for relying on "ineffective self reporting for age assurance."

Replika CEO Dmytro Klochko told Mashable in 2025 that the platform is intended only for users over 18 — and the company's Terms of Service confirms this — but as Ruiz writes, "Klochko acknowledged that some users attempt to bypass 'strict protocols' for preventing underage access."

Whether Apple's new policy will adequately address such concerns is yet to be determined, as all apps must complete the declarations by Jan. 12, 2027.

Meanwhile, the global debate over age verification remains one of the major topics concerning Big Tech and teens today — along with social media bans, of course.

#428. Chernobyl’s Dogs May Be Evolving, but Scientists Don’t Know Why

The dogs living near the disaster site of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant are not like other dogs—at least as far as their genomes go. In recent years, researchers uncovered a unique genetic profile among this population, but what’s driven this distinction remained unclear.

The explanation that’s perhaps most tantalizing to a sci-fi author is that the persistent radiation at the nuclear site has caused mutations to accumulate in the dogs’ genomes. But there are other ways a population’s genetics can change over time, such as random drift or natural selection. A recent study published in the scientific journal Genes revisited these pups, searching for genetic patterns pointing to one of these processes.

The researchers compared the DNA from dogs living in the area right around the nuclear plant with genetic material from dogs living in the city of Chernobyl, about 16 kilometers away. They also compared these canines to other global dog populations. The contrast alone was extreme. The dogs in Chernobyl city “are more genetically similar to dogs in the Galapagos Islands than they are to the dog population” at the nuclear plant, said Megan Dillon, a postdoctoral researcher at North Carolina State University and first author of the study.

But more striking still, the comparison revealed that random chance alone could not explain the differences between the dog populations. Instead, it seems the dogs at the nuclear site have been experiencing natural selection.

“When I was first doing those analyzes, I had to kind of pause and was like, ‘Wow, I have to make sure I'm doing all of this right,’ because this is very interesting, very surprising,” Dillon said.

Not only did the dogs seem to be evolving, but some of the genomic regions under the highest selective pressure were associated with functions such as DNA repair, immunity, and cell survival. In other words, certain genetic differences in the dogs from the plant could be relevant for coping with environmental stress.

Instead of being mutations, these genomic variants likely already existed among local dogs but became more common in the population over the past 40 years. “These dog populations already had this high degree of genetic diversity,” Dillon said. “Maybe this founding population at the power plant had the kind of genetic toolkit to endure and survive in these harsh conditions. It’s not necessarily that they were being bombarded with new mutations.”

Taken together, the results support the hypothesis that natural selection contributed to the difference seen in the dogs at Chernobyl compared to other populations. What remains unclear is which environmental factors favored these variants and whether they provide any specific advantage. “Even though we found this evidence of selection and it is around these biologically relevant genes, we still cannot say that this is tied to the exposures that the dogs have faced,” Dillon noted.

Radiation at the disaster site might seem like the easiest explanation to point to, but there are many other selective pressures this dog population has faced since nuclear meltdown. Chernobyl’s dogs are descended from pets left behind during the evacuations. Since then, they’ve persisted through Ukraine’s harsh winters and weathered other pollutants including heavy metals and pesticides also deposited in the area. “A lot of these contaminants have similar signatures and similar pathology,” Dillon said. “There are just too many different things to really be able to tease apart a single variable.”

The researchers also don’t have access to longitudinal samples that would show exactly how this population has changed over time. “It's almost like looking at a single still image and trying to figure out what came before it,” said Matthew Breen, a professor of genomics at North Carolina State University and the study’s senior author. “Those first few years were probably the most critical period—if they were selected, that's when that selection process would have happened.”

It’s not possible to go back and get samples from the dogs who lived there in 1986, a time when no organism—not even a bacterium—had its full genome sequenced. Breen was a graduate student in England then. “I was involved in a project driving around the Welsh mountain hills, collecting sheep from the pastures because the radioactive cloud had blown over Western Europe,” he recalled. There wasn’t anything to see in the data gathered then, but the technology has evolved, and those sheep had also not been living at the center of a nuclear meltdown for generations.

Nearly four decades after the accident, the Chernobyl exclusion zone has also become a refuge for wildlife. Wolves, deer, wild boars, and lynx now roam the area—a return that researchers largely attribute to the decline in human activity. Among some of these residents, such as the wolf population, researchers have also observed similar genomic distinctions to those seen in the dogs.

“It really demonstrates the resilience of nature to catastrophic events caused by humans,” Breen said. “You push something in one direction, it can respond to that and either push back or deviate its path going forward. I think this is what we're seeing here.”
